claim: More than half of the entire adult human population is latently infected with human cytomegalovirus (HCMV).
source: More than half of the entire adult human population and over 90% of the elderly in developing countries are latently infected with the human cytomegalovirus (HCMV, human betaherpesvirus 5 [HHV-5]; NCBI taxonomy ID 10359) (Fowler et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fowler et al., 2022

claim: Over 90% of the elderly in developing countries are latently infected with HCMV.
source: More than half of the entire adult human population and over 90% of the elderly in developing countries are latently infected with the human cytomegalovirus (HCMV, human betaherpesvirus 5 [HHV-5]; NCBI taxonomy ID 10359) (Fowler et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fowler et al., 2022

claim: More than half of all immune parameters are altered in HCMV-infected individuals.
source: Accordingly, more than half of all immune parameters are altered in HCMV-infected individuals (Brodin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brodin et al., 2015

claim: The depletion of CD4+ cells together with IFNγ results in CMV reactivation in more than 75% of animals.
source: Accordingly, the depletion of CD4 + cells together with IFNγ results in CMV reactivation in more than 75% of animals (Polić et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Polić et al., 1998

claim: The absence of IFN-induced signaling renders mice extremely vulnerable to CMV infections.
source: In accordance with the relevance of IFNs, the absence of IFN-induced signaling renders mice extremely vulnerable to CMV infections (Gil et al., 2001; Le Trilling et al., 2018; Strobl et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gil et al., 2001; Le Trilling et al., 2018; Strobl et al., 2005

claim: HCMV-specific CD4+ T cells produce IFNγ, TNFα, and granzyme B.
source: HCMV-specific CD4 + T cells were shown to produce IFNγ, TNFα, and granzyme B (Gamadia et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to Gamadia et al., 2004

claim: HCMV-specific CD4+ T cells lyse HCMV antigen-expressing cells in vitro.
source: HCMV-specific CD4 + T cells were shown to produce IFNγ, TNFα, and granzyme B (Gamadia et al., 2004) and to lyse HCMV antigen-expressing cells in vitro (van Leeuwen et al., 2006; van Leeuwen et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to van Leeuwen et al., 2006; van Leeuwen et al., 2004

claim: CD4+ T cell-mediated immunity is crucial for CMV control in mouse models in vivo.
source: Accordingly, CD4 + T cell-mediated immunity is crucial for CMV control in mouse models in vivo (Jonjić et al., 1989; Jonjić et al., 1990; Walton et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to Jonjić et al., 1989; Jonjić et al., 1990; Walton et al., 2008

claim: CD4+ T cells are fundamental to prevent HCMV reactivation in immunocompromised patients receiving solid organ allografts.
source: Furthermore, CD4 + T cells are fundamental to prevent HCMV reactivation in immunocompromised patients receiving solid organ allografts (Lim et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lim et al., 2020

claim: Insufficient CD4+ T cell levels in transplant recipients are associated with recurrent HCMV reactivation, end-organ disease, and an increased likelihood of lethal infections.
source: CD4 + T cells are fundamental to prevent HCMV reactivation in immunocompromised patients receiving solid organ allografts (Lim et al., 2020) or hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT), while insufficient CD4 + T cell levels in transplant recipients are associated with recurrent HCMV reactivation, end-organ disease, and an increased likelihood of lethal infections (Einsele et al., 1993; Gabanti et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Einsele et al., 1993; Gabanti et al., 2015

claim: CIITA is the essential and sufficient master regulator of the transcription of the genes in the HLA-II locus.
source: Constitutive as well as IFNγ-induced HLA-II expression are both mediated by the class II transactivator (CIITA), which is the essential and sufficient master regulator of the transcription of the genes in the HLA-II locus.
evidence: Draws from established scientific consensus about CIITA function

claim: CIITA and its co-factors control the expression of the classical HLA-II molecules DR, DQ, DP, the non-classical HLA-II peptidome editors DM and DO, and the invariant chain (Ii, also known as CD74).
source: Accordingly, CIITA and its co-factors control the expression of the classical HLA-II molecules DR, DQ, DP, the non-classical HLA-II peptidome editors DM and DO, and the invariant chain (Ii, also known as CD74) (Boss and Jensen, 2003; Ting and Trowsdale, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boss and Jensen, 2003; Ting and Trowsdale, 2002

claim: The absence of functional CIITA results in a loss of HLA-II presentation, leading to a hereditary immunodeficiency called type II bare lymphocyte syndrome (BLS).
source: The absence of functional CIITA results in a loss of HLA-II presentation, leading to a hereditary immunodeficiency called type II bare lymphocyte syndrome (BLS) that causes an extreme vulnerability to infections.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about BLS

claim: BLS patients frequently suffer from severe, persistent HCMV infections.
source: In accordance with the relevance of CD4 + T cells and CIITA-driven HLA-II presentation, BLS patients frequently suffer from severe, persistent HCMV infections (Elhasid and Etzioni, 1996; Klein et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to Elhasid and Etzioni, 1996; Klein et al., 1993

claim: pUS28 is among the few viral proteins abundantly expressed during both productive replication as well as experimental and natural latency.
source: Importantly, pUS28 is among the few viral proteins abundantly expressed during both productive replication as well as experimental and natural latency (Beisser et al., 2001; Cheung et al., 2006; Goodrum et al., 2002; Krishna et al., 2018; Krishna et al., 2017a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Beisser et al., 2001; Cheung et al., 2006; Goodrum et al., 2002; Krishna et al., 2018; Krishna et al., 2017a

claim: IFNγ induced the upregulation of HLA-DP on the surface of HCMV-permissive fibroblasts.
source: IFNγ induced the upregulation of HLA-DP on the surface of HCMV-permissive fibroblasts (Figure 1A and B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B

claim: IFNα and TNFα treatment did not induce HLA-DP upregulation on fibroblasts.
source: IFNγ induced the upregulation of HLA-DP on the surface of HCMV-permissive fibroblasts (Figure 1A and B), whereas this was not the case after treatment with IFNα or TNFα (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Longer periods of IFNγ incubation led to an increase of HLA-DP and HLA-DR on the cell surface.
source: Longer periods of IFNγ incubation led to an increase of HLA-DP and HLA-DR on the cell surface (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The upregulation of HLA-DP by IFNγ was prevented in HCMV-infected cells.
source: In clear contrast to uninfected fibroblasts, the upregulation of HLA-DP by IFNγ was prevented in HCMV-infected cells (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E

claim: HCMV mutants lacking the US2-6 or the US2-11 gene region showed the same inhibitory phenotype on HLA-DP upregulation as wild-type HCMV.
source: Interestingly, the same inhibitory phenotype was observed upon infection with HCMV mutants lacking the US2-6 or the US2-11 gene region (Figure 1D and E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E

claim: HCMV encodes so far unknown antagonists of IFNγ-induced HLA-DP presentation located outside of the US2-11 gene region.
source: These data indicate that HCMV encodes so far unknown antagonists of IFNγ-induced HLA-DP presentation located outside of the US2-11 gene region.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing that US2-11 deletion mutants still inhibit HLA-DP

claim: pUS28 was identified as a candidate antagonist of HLA-DP induction in a screen of HCMV genes.
source: The screen provided candidates for the observed antagonism of HLA-DP induction, including pUS9, pUS19, pp65-UL83, and pUS28.
evidence: Supported by experimental screening data described in the text and Figure 2A

claim: pUS28 reproducibly diminished CIITA-induced HLA-DP surface expression.
source: Validation experiments substantiated that pUS28 was reproducibly capable of significantly diminishing CIITA-induced HLA-DP surface expression (Figure 2B and data not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: pUS28 significantly diminished the cell surface expression of HLA-DR.
source: Similar to its effect on HLA-DP, pUS28 also significantly diminished the cell surface expression of the presenting molecules HLA-DR (Figure 2C and D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D

claim: pUS28 significantly diminished the cell surface expression of HLA-DQ.
source: Similar to its effect on HLA-DP, pUS28 also significantly diminished the cell surface expression of the presenting molecules HLA-DR (Figure 2C and D) and HLA-DQ (Figure 2D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: pUS28 significantly diminished the cell surface expression of HLA-DM.
source: pUS28 also significantly diminished the cell surface expression of the presenting molecules HLA-DR (Figure 2C and D) and HLA-DQ (Figure 2D) as well as the peptide editor HLA-DM (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: pUS28 dose-dependently inhibited surface levels of HLA-DR at different levels of CIITA abundance.
source: While increasing amounts of CIITA dose-dependently drove HLA-DP and HLA-DR expression in transfected cells, pUS28 significantly and dose-dependently inhibited surface levels of HLA-DR (Figure 2E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: pUS28 dose-dependently inhibited surface levels of HLA-DP at different levels of CIITA abundance.
source: While increasing amounts of CIITA dose-dependently drove HLA-DP and HLA-DR expression in transfected cells, pUS28 significantly and dose-dependently inhibited surface levels of HLA-DR (Figure 2E) and HLA-DP (Figure 2F), at different levels of CIITA abundance.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F

claim: The levels of CIITA mRNA remained unaltered in the presence of pUS28.
source: Irrespective of the presence or absence of pUS28, the levels of tagged as well as untagged CIITA mRNA remained unaltered (Figure 3A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: pUS28 co-expression drastically reduced CIITA protein amounts.
source: In contrast to the unchanged mRNA levels of CIITA, a parallel evaluation of CIITA protein amounts revealed a drastic reduction upon pUS28 co-expression (Figure 3B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: pUS28 has a post-transcriptional effect on CIITA.
source: In contrast to the unchanged mRNA levels of CIITA, a parallel evaluation of CIITA protein amounts revealed a drastic reduction upon pUS28 co-expression (Figure 3B), suggesting a post-transcriptional effect of pUS28 on CIITA.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mRNA levels remain unchanged while protein levels decrease

claim: The CIITA down-modulating capacity of pUS28 is specific for CIITA and does not affect control proteins such as EYFP.
source: The CIITA down-modulating capacity of pUS28 was observed with different plasmid preparations (Figure 3C), and was specific for CIITA, since control proteins such as the enhanced yellow fluorescent protein (EYFP) remained unaffected (Figure 3C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The effect of pUS28 on CIITA is not a general capacity of viral chemokine receptor homologs, as pUS27 did not decrease CIITA protein amounts.
source: The effect on CIITA was also not an overarching capacity of viral chemokine receptor homologs, since the protein pUS27, a GPCR encoded by the neighboring gene in the viral genome, did not decrease CIITA protein amounts (Figure 3D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: pUS27 did not decrease HLA-DP surface levels.
source: The effect on CIITA was also not an overarching capacity of viral chemokine receptor homologs, since the protein pUS27, a GPCR encoded by the neighboring gene in the viral genome, did not decrease CIITA protein amounts (Figure 3D) or HLA-DP surface levels (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E

claim: Mass spectrometry analyses confirmed the significant downregulation of CIITA by pUS28.
source: These unbiased MS analyses confirmed the significant downregulation of CIITA by pUS28 (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4F

claim: pUS28 led to a significant upregulation of IL-6.
source: In agreement with previous data, pUS28 led to a significant upregulation of IL-6 (Slinger et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Slinger et al., 2010

claim: pUS28 attenuated AP-1 components including JunD.
source: In agreement with previous data, pUS28 led to a significant upregulation of IL-6 (Slinger et al., 2010), and attenuated AP-1 components (Krishna et al., 2019) (here JunD) (Figure 4D and E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and E and citation to Krishna et al., 2019

claim: CD74 was significantly induced by CIITA, unless pUS28 was co-expressed.
source: Conversely, CD74 - the invariant chain required for proper maturation and loading of HLA class II molecules - was significantly induced by CIITA, unless pUS28 was co-expressed (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G

claim: The negative effect of pUS28 on CIITA-driven CD74 expression was confirmed by flow cytometry.
source: The negative effect of pUS28 on CIITA-driven CD74 expression was confirmed by flow cytometry (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H

claim: pUS28 elicits the negative effect on CIITA target genes independent of their genomic localization in the MHC-II locus.
source: In contrast to several other CIITA-regulated genes, CD74 is not encoded by the HLA-II locus on chromosome 6. Thus, the fact that pUS28 prevents CIITA-induced CD74 induction suggests that pUS28 elicits the negative effect on CIITA target genes independent of their genomic localization in the MHC-II locus.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that pUS28 affects CD74, which is not in the HLA-II locus

claim: HLA-DP cell surface levels were significantly decreased upon pUS28 induction in doxycycline-inducible fibroblasts.
source: While doxycycline treatment in parental and pUS27-expressing fibroblasts had no significant effect on the IFNγ-induced HLA-DP expression, HLA-DP cell surface levels were significantly decreased upon pUS28 induction (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: Wild-type HCMV significantly decreased the percentage of HLA-DP- and HLA-DR-positive cells compared to mock-treated cells.
source: In accordance with aforementioned data, wt HCMV significantly decreased the percentage of HLA-DP- and HLA-DR-positive cells in comparison to mock-treated cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data described in the text and Figure 5B and C

claim: ΔUS28-HCMV showed an impaired ability to downregulate HLA-II compared to wild-type HCMV.
source: In contrast, ΔUS28-HCMV showed an impaired ability to downregulate HLA-II (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C

claim: pM33 and pUS28 both downregulate human and mouse CIITA.
source: We found that pM33 and pUS28 both downregulate human and mouse CIITA, suggesting an evolutionarily conserved function.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and E

claim: The ability of pUS28 to decrease HLA class II expression is evolutionarily conserved.
source: We found that pM33 and pUS28 both downregulate human and mouse CIITA, suggesting an evolutionarily conserved function.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both pUS28 and its MCMV homolog pM33 downregulate CIITA

claim: pUS28 and CIITA physically interact and form complexes.
source: The IP of pUS28 co-purified CIITA (Figure 6A, upper panel) and vice versa (Figure 6A, lower panel), indicating that both proteins form physical complexes.
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A

claim: pUS28 reduces the half-life of CIITA.
source: Despite the inherently short half-life of CIITA (Schnappauf et al., 2003), we observed a more rapid CIITA decay when pUS28 was co-expressed (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase assay data shown in Figure 6B

claim: A panel of inhibitors targeting different cellular degradation pathways failed to significantly and reproducibly restore CIITA levels in pUS28-expressing cells.
source: Intriguingly, a panel of inhibitors targeting different cellular degradation pathways (e.g. the inhibitors of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway MG-132 and Bortezomib, the inhibitors of UBA3-dependent neddylation blocking cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase activity MLN4924 and TAS4464, the autophagy inhibitors bafilomycin and 3-MA, the inhibitors of lysosomal acidification chloroquine and ammonium chloride, the pan-caspase inhibitor Z-VAD-FMK, the protease inhibitors Pepstatin A, E-64, PMSF, and a pan-protease inhibitor cocktail, as well as the dynamin inhibitor Dynasore and the convertase inhibitor Decanoyl-RVKR-CMK) all failed to significantly and reproducibly restore CIITA levels in pUS28-expressing cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 4 and data not shown)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4

claim: pUS28 reduces CIITA levels either by redundant or unusual degradation processes.
source: all failed to significantly and reproducibly restore CIITA levels in pUS28-expressing cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 4 and data not shown), implying that pUS28 reduces CIITA levels either by redundant or unusual degradation processes.
evidence: Inferred from the failure of multiple degradation pathway inhibitors to restore CIITA

claim: R129A-pUS28 is a mutant that harbors a single amino acid substitution at position 129 (arginine to alanine) within the canonical DRY motif, abrogating G-protein signaling without compromising the subcellular localization or internalization.
source: The latter is a well-studied mutant of pUS28 that harbors a single amino acid substitution at position 129 (arginine to alanine) within the canonical DRY motif, abrogating G-protein signaling without compromising the subcellular localization or internalization (Waldhoer et al., 2003; visualized in Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Waldhoer et al., 2003 and visualization in Figure 7A

claim: Both wt-pUS28 and R129A-pUS28 diminished CIITA protein levels.
source: Both pUS28 variants diminished CIITA protein levels (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B

claim: The intracellular C terminus of pUS28 is indispensable for CIITA degradation.
source: Conversely, the intracellular C terminus turned out to be indispensable for the CIITA degradation (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C

claim: R129A-pUS28 and wt-pUS28 similarly diminished the surface expression of HLA-DP.
source: In accordance with these findings, R129A-pUS28 and wt-pUS28 similarly diminished the surface expression of HLA-DP (Figure 7D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D

claim: R129A-pUS28 and wt-pUS28 similarly diminished the surface expression of HLA-DR.
source: In accordance with these findings, R129A-pUS28 and wt-pUS28 similarly diminished the surface expression of HLA-DP (Figure 7D) and HLA-DR (Figure 7E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E

claim: The mutant lacking the C terminus (US28-ΔC) did not diminish HLA-DP surface expression.
source: while the mutant lacking the C terminus (US28-ΔC) did not (Figure 7F and G)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F

claim: The mutant lacking the C terminus (US28-ΔC) did not diminish HLA-DR surface expression.
source: while the mutant lacking the C terminus (US28-ΔC) did not (Figure 7F and G)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G

claim: pUS28 targets CIITA through its C terminus.
source: while the mutant lacking the C terminus (US28-ΔC) did not (Figure 7F and G), indicating that pUS28 targets CIITA through its C terminus.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that C-terminal deletion abolishes CIITA targeting

claim: pUS28-ΔC co-purified CIITA in immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: In IP experiments, pUS28-ΔC co-purified CIITA (Figure 7H)
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7H

claim: The lack of the C terminus of pUS28 did not impair the physical interaction with CIITA but rather affected the degradation machinery.
source: In IP experiments, pUS28-ΔC co-purified CIITA (Figure 7H), suggesting that the lack of the C terminus of pUS28 did not impair the physical interaction with CIITA but rather affected the degradation machinery.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that pUS28-ΔC still binds CIITA but does not degrade it

claim: Amino acids in proximity to the transmembrane domain 7 of pUS28 were required for downregulation of CIITA.
source: Further investigations of the C-terminal part of pUS28 revealed that amino acids in proximity to the transmembrane domain 7 were required for downregulation of CIITA as only a mutant lacking the whole C terminus completely lost the capability to target CIITA (Figure 7I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7I

claim: HCMV-specific CD4+ T cells from HCMV-positive individuals vigorously responded to CIITA-expressing cells.
source: HCMV-specific CD4 + T cells from HCMV-positive individuals vigorously responded to CIITA-expressing cells, but not to control cells that did not express CIITA (Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B

claim: HCMV-specific CD4+ T cells did not respond to control cells that did not express CIITA.
source: HCMV-specific CD4 + T cells from HCMV-positive individuals vigorously responded to CIITA-expressing cells, but not to control cells that did not express CIITA (Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B

claim: The response of HCMV-specific CD4+ T cells to CIITA-expressing cells indicates a specific HLA-II-dependent T cell activation.
source: HCMV-specific CD4 + T cells from HCMV-positive individuals vigorously responded to CIITA-expressing cells, but not to control cells that did not express CIITA (Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1), indicating a specific HLA-II-dependent T cell activation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that T cells respond only to CIITA-expressing cells

claim: In the presence of pUS28 or R129A-pUS28, the immune recognition of CIITA-expressing, antigen-loaded cells by HCMV-specific CD4+ T cells was significantly reduced.
source: In the presence of pUS28 or the mutant R129A-pUS28, the immune recognition of CIITA-expressing, antigen-loaded cells by HCMV-specific CD4 + T cells was significantly reduced (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B

claim: Supernatants from HCMV-specific CD4+ T cells stimulated with CIITA-expressing cells strongly inhibited HCMV-induced EGFP expression.
source: Supernatants from HCMV-specific CD4 + T cells stimulated with CIITA-expressing cells strongly inhibited HCMV-induced EGFP expression
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C and D

claim: Supernatants derived from CD4+ T cells stimulated in the presence of pUS28 showed diminished antiviral activity.
source: while supernatants derived from CD4 + T cells stimulated in the presence of pUS28 showed diminished antiviral activity (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C and D

claim: pUS28 inhibits the CIITA-driven and HLA-II-dependent CD4+ T cell activation in terms of the production of antiviral cytokines.
source: These data demonstrate that pUS28 inhibits the CIITA-driven and HLA-II-dependent CD4 + T cell activation in terms of the production of antiviral cytokines.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that pUS28 reduces T cell activation and antiviral activity of supernatants

claim: pUS28 acts as calcium-mobilizing beta chemokine receptor.
source: Briefly after its discovery as HCMV-encoded GPCR (Chee et al., 1990), the striking homology of pUS28 to human CX3CR1 was noticed (Gao et al., 1993) and its functionality as calcium-mobilizing beta chemokine receptor was documented (Gao and Murphy, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gao and Murphy, 1994

claim: pUS28 can act as a co-factor for HIV entry.
source: For example, it can act as a co-factor for the HIV entry (Pleskoff et al., 1997)
evidence: Supported by citation to Pleskoff et al., 1997

claim: pUS28 mediates G protein-coupled intracellular signaling.
source: it mediates G protein-coupled intracellular signaling (Billstrom et al., 1998)
evidence: Supported by citation to Billstrom et al., 1998

claim: pUS28 sequesters RANTES/MCP-1.
source: it sequesters RANTES/MCP-1 (Bodaghi et al., 1998)
evidence: Supported by citation to Bodaghi et al., 1998

claim: pUS28 serves as fractalkine receptor.
source: and serves as fractalkine receptor (Burg et al., 2015; Kledal et al., 1998)
evidence: Supported by citations to Burg et al., 2015; Kledal et al., 1998

claim: pUS28 mediates vascular smooth muscle cell migration.
source: it mediates vascular smooth muscle cell migration (Burg et al., 2015; Kledal et al., 1998; Melnychuk et al., 2004; Streblow et al., 1999; Streblow et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to Burg et al., 2015; Kledal et al., 1998; Melnychuk et al., 2004; Streblow et al., 1999; Streblow et al., 2003

claim: pUS28 may act as an oncogene or onco-modulatory protein.
source: and it may act as an oncogene or onco-modulatory protein (Bongers et al., 2010; Maussang et al., 2006; Slinger et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bongers et al., 2010; Maussang et al., 2006; Slinger et al., 2010

claim: pUS28 targets MNDA/PYHIN3 and IFI16/PYHIN2 for rapid degradation.
source: Elegant work by the Sinclair laboratory revealed that pUS28, besides its function as GPCR and latency regulator, targets certain host proteins such as MNDA/PYHIN3 and IFI16/PYHIN2 for rapid degradation.
evidence: Draws from work by the Sinclair laboratory as described in the text

claim: The degradation of MNDA/PYHIN3 and IFI16/PYHIN2 by pUS28 was dependent on GPCR signaling.
source: In contrast to the effect on CIITA shown here, however, this degradation was dependent on GPCR signaling as indicated by the restoration of target protein levels when R129 was mutated (Elder et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Elder et al., 2019

claim: Latently infected primary human CD14+ monocytes exhibit less HLA-DR on the surface compared to uninfected cells.
source: Importantly, Elder et al., 2019 and Slobedman et al., 2002 showed that latently infected primary human CD14 + monocytes and human fetal liver hematopoietic cells exhibit less HLA-DR on the surface compared to uninfected cells (Elder et al., 2019; Slobedman et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Elder et al., 2019 and Slobedman et al., 2002

claim: There is an inverse correlation between HCMV transcripts and CD74 as well as HLA-II expression in CD14+ monocytes.
source: which is very well in line with findings by Shnayder et al., 2020 who showed an inverse correlation between HCMV transcripts and CD74 as well as HLA-II expression in CD14 + monocytes (Shnayder et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shnayder et al., 2020

claim: The deletion of the MCMV US28 homolog M33 results in altered MHC-I presentation in an allotype-specific manner.
source: Recent work with the MCMV model showed that the deletion of the US28 homolog M33 results in altered MHC-I presentation in an allotype-specific manner (H-2Ld and H-2Kd being downregulated in an M33-dependent manner, but not H-2Dd) (White et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to White et al., 2022

claim: HCMV counteracts IFNγ-induced gene expression, partly by inducing the proteasomal degradation of JAK1.
source: Work by Miller et al., 1998 showed that HCMV counteracts IFNγ-induced gene expression, partly by inducing the proteasomal degradation of JAK1, leading to diminished CIITA and HLA-DRα induction when HCMV-infected cells are exposed to IFNγ (Miller et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Miller et al., 1998

claim: HCMV targets constitutive as well as induced CIITA-dependent HLA-II expression at multiple levels by a multipronged attack.
source: Furthermore, HCMV targets constitutive as well as induced CIITA-dependent HLA-II expression at multiple levels by a multipronged attack, comprising the inhibition of (I) IFN-JAK-STAT signaling (Le et al., 2008; Le Trilling et al., 2020; Miller et al., 1998), (II) constitutive CIITA transcription (Lee et al., 2011; Sandhu and Buchkovich, 2020), (III) CIITA protein stability (as shown here), and (IV) HLA-DR degradation and translocation (Hegde and Johnson, 2003; Hegde et al., 2002; Tomazin et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations and data from this study

claim: pUS28 may shield latently infected cells from HLA-II-restricted CD4+ T lymphocytes.
source: Based on the aforementioned role of pUS28 for HCMV latency, it is tempting to speculate that pUS28 may shield latently infected cells from HLA-II-restricted CD4 + T lymphocytes.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the role of pUS28 in latency and its effect on HLA-II

claim: HLA-DR+NKG2C+ memory NK cells are mediators of viral control in transplanted patients.
source: Another intriguing possibility is that a relevant fraction of the HLA-II-mediated CD4 + T cell activation might be elicited by cells that are resistant to HCMV infections, such as the recently described HLA-DR +NKG2C+memory NK cells (Costa-García et al., 2019), which have been shown to be mediators of viral control in transplanted patients (Davis et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Costa-García et al., 2019 and Davis et al., 2015
